quiz.question: Two firms set prices. In industry $A$, each firm's cost is common knowledge; in industry $B$, each firm knows only its own cost. Which statement correctly describes the difference?

answerOptions.text: In $A$ there is no residual uncertainty, so neither firm needs a best response.
answerOptions.rationale: Common knowledge of costs is still a game: each firm must anticipate the other's price. Residual uncertainty remains about actions (and any randomisation).

answerOptions.text: In $A$, residual uncertainty is only about what the other will do; in $B$, each firm is also uncertain about what the other knows.
answerOptions.rationale: Complete information: the game structure and payoffs are common knowledge. Incomplete information: private costs mean uncertainty about what others know.

answerOptions.text: Mixed strategies already capture $B$'s cost uncertainty, so the two industries are strategically equivalent.
answerOptions.rationale: Mixing is randomisation over own actions, not private information about payoffs. Incomplete information requires signals and interim beliefs.

answerOptions.text: Industry $B$ cannot be analysed until costs are revealed, because Bayesian games require realised payoffs to be common knowledge.
answerOptions.rationale: Bayesian games are designed for private information. The distribution $f$ and the payoff functions are common knowledge; realised costs need not be.

quiz.hint: What residual uncertainty remains in each industry?

quiz.question: A student argues that a Bayesian game is really a complete-information game, because the joint distribution $f$ and the payoff functions $u_i$ are common knowledge. Where does the argument fail?

answerOptions.text: The argument is correct once $f$ is common knowledge; private signals then add nothing.
answerOptions.rationale: Common knowledge of the information structure is not common knowledge of realised signals. Players still do not observe $x_{-i}$.

answerOptions.text: The argument fails only when signals are correlated; independence would restore complete information.
answerOptions.rationale: Independence affects whether $x_i$ updates beliefs about $x_{-i}$, not whether $x_{-i}$ is observed. Incomplete information remains either way.

answerOptions.text: The argument fails because $f$ and the $u_i$ are each player's private information; only action sets are common knowledge.
answerOptions.rationale: The lecture states the opposite: distributions and payoffs are common knowledge. What is private is the realised signal $x_i$.

answerOptions.text: Complete information requires that realised payoffs be common knowledge. Each player observes only $x_i$, so there remains uncertainty about what others know.
answerOptions.rationale: Player $i$ sees only $x_i$. The rules of the game are common knowledge; the realisation of private information is not.

quiz.hint: Distinguish knowing the information structure from observing the realisation.

quiz.question: In the incomplete-information Battle of the Sexes, Player 2 observes $x_2 \in \{M,N\}$ while Player 1 does not. If Player 1 plays $O$, why is Player 2's best response $OF$, independently of $p$?

answerOptions.text: $OF$ is the mixed strategy that plays $O$ with probability $p$ and $F$ with probability $1-p$ after every signal.
answerOptions.rationale: $OF$ is a pure strategy: $O$ after $M$ and $F$ after $N$. It is not a mixture, and $p$ is Player 1's belief, not Player 2's mix.

answerOptions.text: Player 2 cannot condition on $x_2$, so $OF$ means matching $O$ whenever Player 1 plays $O$.
answerOptions.rationale: Strategies map own signals to actions. They cannot condition on the opponent's simultaneous action, but they can condition on own private signal.

answerOptions.text: After $M$, matching with $O$ is best; after $N$, mismatching with $F$ is best. Player 2 observes $x_2$, so this contingent plan is available; $p$ is Player 1's uncertainty, not Player 2's.
answerOptions.rationale: Player 2 knows whether they want to meet. Notation $OF$ means play $O$ when $M$ and $F$ when $N$. Because the signal is observed, the best reply does not average using $p$.

answerOptions.text: $OO$ is also a best response to $O$ whenever $p$ is high, because then signal $N$ is unlikely.
answerOptions.rationale: That would be Player 1's problem. Player 2 observes $N$ when it occurs and then strictly prefers $F$ against $O$; a high $p$ does not make $OO$ optimal.

quiz.hint: Who observes $x_2$, and who is uncertain about it?

quiz.question: Signals are independent, so $f(x_{-i}|x_i) = f_{-i}(x_{-i})$. Why does player $i$ still need the marginal $f_{-i}$ when computing interim expected utility?

answerOptions.text: Opponents' strategies $\sigma_{-i}(x_{-i})$ — and possibly $u_i$ itself — still depend on the unknown $x_{-i}$. Independence only says that $x_i$ does not update the distribution of $x_{-i}$.
answerOptions.rationale: The posterior equals the marginal, but $i$ must still average over $x_{-i}$. Payoffs may depend on the full profile $x$ even when signals are independent (independence is not private values).

answerOptions.text: Independence implies private values, so $x_{-i}$ cannot affect $u_i$ and the marginal is redundant.
answerOptions.rationale: Independence is a restriction on $f$, not on $u_i$. Private values ($u_i(a|x)=u_i(a|x_i)$) is a separate condition.

answerOptions.text: Independence forces a uniform posterior $1/|X_{-i}|$, which is all $i$ needs.
answerOptions.rationale: Independence preserves the marginal of $x_{-i}$; it does not flatten that marginal into a uniform distribution.

answerOptions.text: Interim beliefs are undefined until $i$ also observes opponents' actions.
answerOptions.rationale: Interim beliefs are formed after observing $x_i$ and before actions. Independence is enough to write them down.

quiz.hint: What still depends on the unobserved $x_{-i}$?

quiz.question: Why must a Bayes Nash equilibrium strategy be a best response after every signal $x_i$ with $f(x_i)>0$, rather than only after the most likely signals?

answerOptions.text: Only mixed strategies must be optimal at every signal; a pure strategy need only be optimal after the most likely signal.
answerOptions.rationale: The definition applies to all strategies, pure or mixed: no profitable deviation at any signal realisation with positive probability.

answerOptions.text: Nature's draw of $x$ is observed by all players before they choose, so each $x_i$ is commonly known and must be best-replied to publicly.
answerOptions.rationale: Players observe only their own signal at the interim stage, not the full profile $x$.

answerOptions.text: A strategy that is suboptimal after a low-probability signal can still be a BNE, provided it is a best response after all other signals.
answerOptions.rationale: BNE requires a best response at every $x_i \in X_i$ with $f(x_i)>0$, including rare signals.

answerOptions.text: A player who has observed $x_i$ can deviate at that signal alone. If the deviation raises interim payoff, it also raises ex-ante payoff because $f(x_i)>0$.
answerOptions.rationale: Strategies must be optimal at the interim stage. A one-signal deviation is feasible and, if it raises $U_i(\cdot|x_i)$, it raises $V_i$ as well.

quiz.hint: Imagine a profitable deviation used only after one realised signal.

quiz.question: In the transformed Battle of the Sexes, Player 1 has one signal while Player 2 has two. A student says the transformation (strategy sets $S_i=\{\sigma_i:X_i\to\Delta A_i\}$, payoffs $V_i$) is valid for Player 1 but not for Player 2. What is wrong with that claim?

answerOptions.text: The claim is correct: Player 2 must be split into two players, one for each signal, before Nash equilibrium is well-defined.
answerOptions.rationale: Treating types as separate players is a convenient computational device (used later in Cournot), but the transformation already handles multiple signals through $V_i$.

answerOptions.text: Write $V_2 = p\,U_2(\cdot|M)+(1-p)\,U_2(\cdot|N)$. The action after each signal enters only that term, and both weights are positive, so maximising $V_2$ maximises each interim payoff.
answerOptions.rationale: Player 1's single signal makes the coincidence transparent, but the same algebra applies to Player 2. With $f(x_i)>0$, ex-ante NE conditions are exactly the interim BNE conditions.

answerOptions.text: The transformation works for Player 2 only when $p=1/2$, so that the two signals are equally weighted.
answerOptions.rationale: Equal weights are unnecessary. Any $f(x_i)>0$ preserves the ranking of that signal's interim payoff.

answerOptions.text: The transformation works for Player 2 only under private values, which fail here because $N$ does not want to meet.
answerOptions.rationale: The decomposition of $V_i$ does not require private values. Not wanting to meet is just a different payoff function after signal $N$.

quiz.hint: Which term of $V_2$ does the action after $M$ enter?

quiz.question: Player 2's best response is $OF$ against $O$ and $FO$ against $F$, independently of $p$. Player 1 prefers $O$ against $OF$ iff $p>1/3$, and prefers $F$ against $FO$ iff $p>2/3$. If $p=3/4$, which statement is correct?

answerOptions.text: Both $(O, OF)$ and $(F, FO)$ are pure-strategy BNEs.
answerOptions.rationale: At $p=3/4$, both $p>1/3$ and $p>2/3$ hold, so Player 1 is willing to play $O$ against $OF$ and $F$ against $FO$. Each pair is then a mutual best response.

answerOptions.text: Only $(F, FO)$ is a pure-strategy BNE, because $p>2/3$ knocks out $(O, OF)$.
answerOptions.rationale: The cutoff $p>2/3$ is for preferring $F$ against $FO$. Against $OF$, Player 1 still prefers $O$ whenever $p>1/3$, which includes $p=3/4$.

answerOptions.text: There is no pure-strategy BNE, because two candidate profiles cannot both be equilibria.
answerOptions.rationale: Multiple pure BNEs can coexist. That is exactly the case for $p>2/3$.

answerOptions.text: $(O, OO)$ is a BNE, because with $p=3/4$ Player 2 almost surely wants to meet and should always play $O$.
answerOptions.rationale: Player 2's best response to $O$ is $OF$ for any $p$. After $N$, mismatching with $F$ is strictly better; a high $p$ does not justify $OO$.

quiz.question: In the entry game, $(Out, IN)$ is a BNE when $p>2/3$: the low-cost incumbent invests and the entrant stays out. Relative to complete information, why does the high-cost incumbent earn more in this equilibrium?

answerOptions.text: Type $H$ also invests in this BNE, and investment is cheaper for $H$ than for $L$.
answerOptions.rationale: Investment costs $2$ for $H$ and $0$ for $L$. In $(Out, IN)$ only type $L$ invests; $H$ does not.

answerOptions.text: If the entrant observed type $H$, they would still stay out, because $H$'s payoff from Invest is higher than $L$'s.
answerOptions.rationale: Under complete information the entrant would enter against $H$ (who does not invest). That is why $H$ earns only $3$ when type is observed.

answerOptions.text: The entrant cannot condition on type, so stays out against both; type $H$ free-rides on the chance that the incumbent is the investing low-cost type.
answerOptions.rationale: Incomplete information pools the types from the entrant's point of view. Staying out against both yields $H$ a payoff of $8$ rather than $3$.

answerOptions.text: Incomplete information makes Out a dominant strategy for the entrant, so deterrence does not depend on $p$.
answerOptions.rationale: Out is a best response to $IN$ only when $p>2/3$. The other BNE has the entrant coming in against $NN$ for any $p$.

quiz.hint: What would the entrant do if type $H$ were observed?

quiz.question: Complete-information Cournot outcomes are $(10/3, 10/3)$ when both costs are zero and $(14/3, 2/3)$ when Firm 2's cost is $4$. A student guesses that the incomplete-information BNE is just the equal-probability average of these two profiles. What goes wrong?

answerOptions.text: Firm 1's complete-information outputs average to $4$, but that cannot be a best response because $4$ lies outside $[10/3, 14/3]$.
answerOptions.rationale: $4$ is exactly the midpoint of $10/3$ and $14/3$, and it is Firm 1's BNE output. The mistake is not that Firm 1's quantity is infeasible.

answerOptions.text: Low-cost Firm 2's marginal cost rises under incomplete information, which is why $BR_2^L$ shifts inward.
answerOptions.rationale: Type $L$'s cost is still zero. The best-response function $BR_2^L(q_1)=5-q_1/2$ is unchanged; what changes is the $q_1$ that type $L$ faces.

answerOptions.text: The two types of Firm 2 collude, averaging their complete-information outputs to hide costs from Firm 1.
answerOptions.rationale: Types of the same firm do not choose jointly. Each type best-responds separately to Firm 1's single output.

answerOptions.text: Firm 1 does produce $4$, the average of $10/3$ and $14/3$; but each type of Firm 2 best-responds to that single $q_1=4$, yielding $3$ and $1$, not the complete-information outputs $10/3$ and $2/3$.
answerOptions.rationale: Firm 1 has one action against both types. Type $L$ then faces a more aggressive rival ($4>10/3$) and cuts output; type $H$ faces a less aggressive rival ($4<14/3$) and expands. Averaging the two complete-information equilibria misses this best-response adjustment.

quiz.hint: Firm 1 chooses one quantity; each type of Firm 2 reacts to that quantity.

quiz.question: Under unanimity, both jurors vote sincerely. Why may a juror who received signal $i$ still strictly prefer to vote $C$, even when $q$ is close to $1$?

answerOptions.text: Sincere voting fails only when signals are imprecise ($q$ near $1/2$), because then own signal $i$ is weak evidence of innocence.
answerOptions.rationale: The cutoff is independent of $q$. Even a precise $i$ signal is cancelled by the pivotal $g$ signal from the other juror.

answerOptions.text: Own vote is pivotal only if the other voted $C$; under sincere voting that means the other saw $g$. The likelihoods $q(1-q)$ cancel, so the posterior equals $\pi$. If $d<\pi/(1-\pi)$, convicting is better.
answerOptions.rationale: Symmetric signals drop out of Bayes' rule, leaving the prior. Then expected payoff from convicting is positive iff $d<\pi/(1-\pi)$, independently of precision.

answerOptions.text: Jurors have conflicting preferences over conviction, so each votes $C$ to impose a cost on the other.
answerOptions.rationale: Conditional on the state, jurors have aligned preferences. The distortion is informational (conditioning on pivotality), not a conflict of interest.

answerOptions.text: Unanimity makes own vote always pivotal, so the juror ignores the other's signal and uses only the prior $\pi$.
answerOptions.rationale: Own vote is pivotal only when the other votes $C$, not always. That event is informative: under sincere voting, it reveals the other's $g$ signal.

quiz.hint: Condition on being pivotal, then apply Bayes' rule.
